chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Fuzayl ibn Yasar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The obligatory and optional prayers are fifty-one rak'ahs in total. Among them are two rak'ahs after 'Atamah (night prayer) prayed while seated, which are counted as one rak'ah while standing. The obligatory among these are seventeen rak'ahs, and the optional are thirty-four rak'ahs.
ai.seo_question: What is the total number of daily rak'ahs in Shia Islam and how are they distributed between obligatory and voluntary prayers?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the canonical count of fifty-one daily rak'ahs, distinguishing between the seventeen obligatory (fard) and thirty-four voluntary (nafl) units. It specifically highlights the jurisprudential nuance of the two-rak'ah Shaf' prayer, noting that while performed seated, it is counted as a single standing unit, thereby integrating it into the total sum. This structure reflects the Shia emphasis on augmenting the five daily prayers with specific supererogatory acts to achieve spiritual completeness.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Ibn Azina, from Fuzeyl Bin Yasaar, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘The Obligatory and the optional (Salāts) are fifty one Rak’at – from it are two Rak’at after the night (to be prayed) seated, counted as one Rak’at prayed while he is standing. The Obligatory from these are seventeen Rak’at, and the optional are thirty four Rak’at’.
en.sarwar: 2. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr from ibn ’Udhaynah from ibn Faddal ibn Yasar who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘

Obligatory and optional Salah (prayer) are fifty-one Rak‘at, of which there are two Rak‘at after al-‘Atmah in a sitting position which are counted as one Rak‘at in a standing position. Obligatory Salah (prayer) are seventeen Rak‘at and optional Salah (prayer) are thirty-four Rak‘at.’”
